topic: Robert Cialdini (1975): 'Door-in-the-Face' — How Getting Told 'NO!' First Tripled Yeses From 17% to 50%!
visual_mode_reason: Robert Cialdini and colleagues' 1975 Arizona State campus walkway experiment — asking passersby for an outrageous 2-year unpaid juvenile-detention commitment (100% said NO!) before 'conceding' to a 2-hour zoo chaperone trip, tripling agreement from 16.7% to 50%! — is classic field social psychology staged outdoors on a sunny campus quad.

primary_case.title: Robert B. Cialdini, Joyce E. Vincent, Stephen K. Lewis, José Catalan, Diane Wheeler & Betty Lee Darby's 1975 'Door-in-the-Face' Campus Field Experiments
primary_case.place: Campus walkways, Arizona State University, Tempe

people.name: Robert B. Cialdini
people.role: 29-year-old Arizona State social psychologist (author of Influence!) who went undercover into fundraising, car sales, and PR training programs to decode real-world persuasion science

people.name: 72 Unsuspecting Campus Walkers (Exp. 1)
people.role: Approached one-by-one outdoors on sunny ASU walkways by student researchers posing as 'County Youth Counseling Program' representatives

people.name: Alvin W. Gouldner
people.role: Sociologist whose universal 'Norm of Reciprocity' (including reciprocal concessions: 'You stepped down, so I'll step up!') Cialdini pinpointed as the engine of the 3x jump

core_facts.fact: Suppose you need volunteers to chaperone a group of juvenile-detention teenagers on a **2-hour Saturday trip to the city zoo**. Walk straight up to strangers on an Arizona State campus walkway (**Small Request Only Control**, Cialdini et al., 1975 *JPSP*) and ask politely: **83.3% turn you down flat — only 16.7% say YES**.

Now try Cialdini's **'Door-in-the-Face' (Rejection-Then-Retraction)** sequence on the exact same walkway: **FIRST**, make an outrageous request almost guaranteed to get a door slammed in your face — *'Will you serve as an unpaid counselor for 2 hours every week for the next **TWO FULL YEARS**?'* Predictably, **100% of walkers (24 out of 24) said NO**.

Immediately — **in the very next breath by the SAME person** — make a graceful concession: *'Okay, I understand — would you at least chaperone a single **2-hour trip to the zoo**?'* Suddenly **50.0% said YES — TRIPLING compliance from 16.7% to 50.0%**.

Wait — was 2 hours just 'looking tiny' next to 2 years (**Perceptual Contrast**), OR did people feel obligated to **match a concession with a concession** (**Reciprocal Concessions**)? In **Experiment 2**, Cialdini added a brilliant third condition (**Two-Requester Control**): Person A asks for the 2-year job ('No!'), walks away, and **Person B** immediately asks for the 2-hour zoo trip.

Look at Experiment 2's proof: Small Request Alone = **25%**; Two Different Requesters (pure perceptual contrast, zero personal concession!) = **dropped to 10.7%**; **Same Requester making a concession = jumped to 55.5%**. The engine wasn't just contrast — it was **Reciprocity**: *'You backed down from 2 years for me, so social fairness demands I step forward from zero to 2 hours for you!'*

Even better (**Cialdini & Ascani, 1976, SRC2**): because Door-in-the-Face targets feel *they negotiated the requester down* and chose freely, **84% actually showed up in person** (vs far higher no-shows under high-pressure sales!), felt *more* responsible for the outcome, and volunteered more again later.

History's wildest real-world case? In 1972, G. Gordon Liddy pitched three Watergate wiretapping budgets to Committee Director Jeb Magruder: **$1,000,000** (kidnapping squads + yachts — 'NO!'), **$500,000** ('Still NO!'), and finally a 'modest concession' of **$250,000** just to bug Democratic HQ at the Watergate — and Magruder sighed *'Okay, $250k'*.

Crucial boundary rule: if Request #1 is **absurdly comical or bad-faith** ('Give me $1,000,000 for bake-sale cookies!'), reciprocity **backfires completely** because people view the retreat as a sleazy trick rather than a genuine concession.

In Cialdini et al.'s (1975) Experiment 1, 0% of campus passersby agreed to 2 years of unpaid juvenile-counseling work, yet immediately retreating to a 2-hour zoo chaperone request lifted agreement to 50.0% (versus 16.7% cold ask).

wow_facts.fact: Ask directly for a 2-hour Saturday zoo favor and **only 17% say yes**; get **100% rejected** on a 2-year favor **ten seconds earlier**, step down politely to the exact same 2-hour zoo trip, and **50% say yes — a 300% explosion**.
wow_facts.why_surprising: Starting with a guaranteed 'NO' tripled real-world 'YES'.

wow_facts.fact: How did 29-year-old Cialdini prove it was **Reciprocity** and not just '2 hours sounding tiny'? Have **Person B** ask for the 2 hours right after **Person A** asked for 2 years — compliance crashed from **55.5% down to 10.7%** because Person B hadn't made you a concession.
wow_facts.why_surprising: Cleanest experimental control in persuasion psychology.

wow_facts.fact: People who agree via Door-in-the-Face don't feel tricked or resentful — in Cialdini's blood-drive follow-up (**1976, SRC2**), they actually **showed up at 84%** and walked away feeling *proud* they steered the deal.
Even Watergate's infamous $250,000 break-in budget got approved via a textbook **$1M — $500k to $250k** Door-in-the-Face retreat.
wow_facts.why_surprising: Persuasion mechanics operating in White House backrooms.

misconceptions.myth: Opening with an astronomical bad-faith demand ('$10 million for a used civic!') triggers Door-in-the-Face magic.
misconceptions.truth: Extreme bad-faith anchors destroy credibility and kill reciprocity — Request #1 must be **large yet plausible and prosocial/genuine** so stepping down feels like a real concession.

They are **exact structural opposites**: Foot-in-the-Door goes *Tiny YES to Big YES* (driven by self-consistency), whereas Door-in-the-Face goes *Big NO to Moderate YES* (driven by reciprocal concessions).

misconceptions.myth: Verbal 'yeses' won on campus walkways evaporate on Saturday morning.
misconceptions.truth: Because targets feel active ownership over the compromise, Cialdini & Ascani (1976) proved behavioral follow-through beats direct requests.

everyday_hooks: Having a charity caller ask for a **$250 annual sustaining membership** ('Oh, I can't right now') and immediately pivot warmly to *'What about a single $15 starter pack?'* — and hearing your own mouth say 'Sure, $15 works!'

Defending your wallet against manipulative sales concessions by asking ONE calm question: ***'Would I say YES to this second offer if I had walked in the door 5 seconds ago without hearing Offer #1?'***
Using ethical two-option framing in salary or scope negotiations (ambitious full package to focused core package).
